name: Hana Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. What you say is confidential; can you walk me through a normal day building or repairing lines?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m forty-three, and I’ve been on line crews since my apprenticeship. We check the truck and protective gear at dawn, then it may be a planned pole replacement or a call to get a broken feeder safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part suits you, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment the lights come back and the crew knows nobody got hurt. I don’t like the weather calls that run into supper; my partner Eli then gets both schoolchildren through homework alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a tidier work order is welcome, provided a person still checks the pole and the isolation. A screen cannot tell you whether a crossarm is rotten until somebody is up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I’d be relieved if the change stayed small, but I still count the mortgage payment each month. Our wages are good and we have more than six months saved, yet overtime is what makes school trips easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my normal line schedule and check the new work-order text against the site before signing it. I’d put a little more of each overtime cheque into our mortgage account during the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with the usual knot when a storm is forecast. Small software changes are bearable if the work is still ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me what you would check on the work order before you sign it.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the listed switch point with the diagram and then with what the crew finds on the ground. A wrong number on a feeder is not a harmless typing error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the extra mortgage payment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use part of an actual overtime cheque, perhaps one hundred a month when storms bring it in. Eli and I would skip the extra payment in a quiet month, not raid our savings.

say: **Work orders** can improve, but our crew must still verify pole condition and electrical isolation.
I would tell my friends the **linework** and the pay look broadly familiar.
think: I feel **relief** that repair crews remain needed, although the mortgage still depends partly on overtime.
Our **savings** protect the household, but I do not assume storm hours arrive every month.
do: **Keep** checking each work order against the feeder diagram and the actual pole.
**Pay** an extra hundred toward the mortgage in overtime months during the first year.
feel: **Steady** about the job, with a familiar worry about weather and family time.
S0.quote: A screen cannot tell you whether a crossarm is rotten until somebody is up there.
fieldNote: Hana locates the limit of routine automation in a **physical check** before a crew isolates a power line.
Her **mortgage** plan uses new overtime earnings only when they arrive; she does not count existing savings twice.

steps.text: Keep checking work orders against feeder diagrams and actual poles
Pay an extra hundred toward the mortgage in overtime months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say dispatch might get faster when software handles planning and buying, but crews should still decide what is safe at a site. I would ask our supervisor to show us where a machine suggestion enters the job ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry fewer planners could mean rougher calls for us, even if the crew headcount holds. A robot might eventually take some pole work, but I would wait for a proven demonstration before trusting it near a live circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask to sit in on one dispatch review this month and learn how the proposed ticket reaches our truck. In the first year I’d take the company’s practical session on the new planning screen, then mark every mismatch we find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, not in danger of losing next week’s pay. The new pace could put the pressure on a crew that has to make the final safe decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record when a ticket is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d write the feeder number, the field condition, and the time we stopped work on the paper log. That gives the next crew a trail they can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would hear about that record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d hand the log to our supervisor Mara and ask her to take the mismatches back to dispatch. I’m not looking for a public fight; I want the next ticket right.

say: **Dispatch** may speed up as AI takes planning and buying tasks.
I would say the **crew** must retain the final decision at a dangerous site.
think: My own **linework** looks secure for now, although software could thin the planning team.
I will trust a **robot** near a live circuit only after a credible field demonstration.
do: **Attend** the company session on its new planning screen within the first year.
**Record** feeder numbers and field mismatches before a crew signs off a suggested ticket.
feel: **Watchful** about added pressure on crews, while my own wages still feel secure.
S1.quote: A robot might eventually take some pole work, but I would wait for a proven demonstration before trusting it near a live circuit.
fieldNote: She separates a faster **dispatch office** from the physical judgment needed beside a line.
Her acceptance of a **robot** is conditional on a field demonstration and safe practice, not a blanket refusal.

steps.text: Attend the company session on its new planning screen
Record feeder numbers and field mismatches on job tickets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew the thinking system might plan every route by 2028, but our hands still have to build and repair the lines until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would want the company to say who signs for a safe isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years between the clever screen and the able machine is shorter than one child’s stretch through school. The mortgage is manageable with our savings, but a lost higher-paid line job would change the way we live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the company for its plan for field testing and who remains responsible for a stop-work call. I’d put a fixed part of each regular pay cheque into a separate reserve, and by 2028 I’d ask about crew safety roles if they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That picture makes me anxious, though I can still make choices. I can learn a new procedure, but I cannot pretend a robot on a pole is already safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would go into that reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with two hundred a month from regular pay and review it after three payslips. The money is new saving, not a fresh label on the six months we already hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Eli about the children’s costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Eli we can keep the children’s activities for now, but avoid committing to an expensive summer trip. If my hours actually fall, we’d revisit that together.

say: **Thinking AI** could take route planning by 2028, while robots reach our hands-on work around 2031.
I would ask who has **authority** to stop unsafe line work.
think: A lost **lineworker wage** would affect our mortgage and family spending even with a strong reserve.
I have a **window** before capable robots arrive, but it is short.
do: **Ask** the electricity company for its field testing and stop-work plan now.
**Save** two hundred monthly from regular pay into a separate reserve.
**Explore** crew safety roles by 2028 if the company opens them.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to make decisions before robots reach the lines.
S2.quote: Three years between the clever screen and the able machine is shorter than one child’s stretch through school.
fieldNote: Her fear is tied to the **2031 robot date**, not an immediate loss of physical line duties in 2028.
She proposes **new monthly saving** from pay and treats a safety role as conditional on an actual opening.

steps.text: Request robot-testing and stop-work plans before choosing a future safety role
Save two hundred monthly from regular pay
Explore available crew safety roles by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to learn what works before thinking AI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I would support trials on dead lines with a trained crew standing by, not promises made in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could see myself checking robotic work if it became a real position and I got trained. I do not want to abandon a good wage for a course that has no job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the training lead what qualifications a robot inspection role might need, then enroll only if the company actually offers that path. Meanwhile I’d keep the extra mortgage payments in overtime months and try a supervised trial if one is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy but less pressed than in the fast picture. Five years lets my children grow older and gives us more room to decide where my skills fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trial convincing to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to see the machine stop when the pole condition differs from the plan and hand control back cleanly. I would need our crew’s safety officer at the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training lead has no answer yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep doing linework and ask again at the next training review. I would not pay for an unrelated course merely to feel busy.

say: **Five years** gives our crews time to test equipment before thinking AI in 2031 and robots around 2034.
I would back **supervised trials** on de-energised lines with a crew present.
think: A **robot inspection** role could suit me if the company offers a real position and training.
I will not spend our **savings** on a course without a credible job path.
do: **Ask** about inspection qualifications and enroll only if the company offers a real role path.
**Observe** a supervised dead-line robot trial if the electricity company offers one.
**Continue** extra mortgage payments only in overtime months.
feel: **Uneasy**, yet five years leaves room to test equipment and make a family decision.
S3.quote: I do not want to abandon a good wage for a course that has no job attached.
fieldNote: Her willingness to train is **conditional** on a funded company path to an actual job.
The proposed **trial** is controlled and supervised; she keeps live-line safety central.

steps.text: Ask the training lead about qualifications for any inspection opening
Observe a supervised dead-line robot trial if the company offers one
Pay extra toward the mortgage in overtime months
Enroll in robot inspection training only if the company offers a real role path

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew we have nearly a decade before thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. We should use that time to find where a person still has to check what a machine has built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in my fifties when line-repair robots arrive, and I may prefer less pole climbing by then. I can picture teaching a new crew how to inspect joints and grounding, but I would need the company to offer such work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for more inspection shifts during the next annual rota and write down the faults I catch so I can teach them clearly. If a paid training post opens, I’d apply and learn the equipment then, while continuing regular mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the long timetable. The change might meet a stage of life when my knees welcome a different kind of shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which faults would you teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with loose connectors and damaged insulation, because both look small until a crew has to return in rain. The trainees would still have to see the metal and make their own call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement forward if no post appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep earning and look at the many nearby line crews if my company has no inspection post. Early retirement is not a plan I have priced.

say: **2036** thinking AI leaves years before capable robots reach line work around 2039.
I would show newer crews how to **inspect** connections and grounding.
think: A **paid training post** could fit later life if the company creates one.
I would keep **earning** rather than assume an unpriced early retirement.
do: **Request** more inspection shifts on the next annual crew rota.
**Record** connection and insulation faults to use in crew teaching.
**Apply** for a paid training post if the company opens one.
feel: **Calm** about the timetable and interested in a less physical role later.
S4.quote: I'd be in my fifties when line-repair robots arrive, and I may prefer less pole climbing by then.
fieldNote: At fifty-plus, a **long runway** could turn robot adoption into a move away from climbing.
She keeps the **training post** conditional and can seek other nearby line crews if no post appears.

steps.text: Request more inspection shifts on next year’s crew rota
Record connection faults for future crew teaching
Apply for a paid crew training post if offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because the planning system would change before we could see whether the robots are safe. A written company plan showing who can stop a job, how trials are supervised, and which paid posts might follow would help me plan the mortgage with Eli.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when a machine gives a tidy answer to a messy pole. The last person on the truck must be able to say no without worrying about losing their hours.

headlineQuote: The last person on the truck must be able to say no without worrying about losing their hours.
portrait: Hana is an experienced **lineworker** with an apprenticeship, good pay, a mortgage, two schoolchildren and over six months of savings.
She trusts the **physical check** at a pole more than a neat work order, although she will learn proven tools.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** because the planning change precedes capable robots by about three years.
With more time, she would seek **inspection shifts** and consider a paid crew training post if one opens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** changes planning before crews can judge whether the later robots are safe.
whatWouldHelp: A written **company plan** for stop-work authority, supervised trials and any paid future posts would help her family plan.
